subtype: Approach: reframing failure as a redirect [Thinking]
passage: Kalyani, you look down, so let old Jagdish tell you about my failed term. Second year, I took six courses and a hostel job. Two courses went badly. I sat on my bed for two days telling myself I was a failure. Then my warden, Mr Bhat, asked me a plain question: "If a friend brought you this marksheet, what would you say?" I said, "That six courses and a job was too much." He said, "So it's not a verdict. It's a message." I went and wrote it out: too heavy, and my way of studying did not suit that load. That was information I could act on. Blame gives you nothing to plan with. Information does.

qa.q: How many courses did Jagdish take in the second year?
What was Jagdish feeling during the two days on the bed?
qa.a: Jagdish felt like a failure, sad and stuck, telling oneself the term proved something bad about oneself.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned the failure into a plan, and why?
qa.a: Jagdish answered the warden's question as if advising a friend, then wrote down that the load was too heavy, because that turned blame into information to act on.

qa.q: How might Mr Bhat have seen Jagdish's marksheet?
qa.a: Mr Bhat treated it as a message, not a verdict, asking a plain question and letting Jagdish reach the answer.

grounding: Shows treating a failed term as information about workload and study methods instead of a verdict, which makes planning possible without self-blame.

subtype: Approach: reframing failure as a redirect [Thinking]
passage: Irawati's results arrived on her phone in the middle of her cousin's engagement in Nashik, between the ring ceremony and lunch. Two subjects failed. Around her, aunties asked about marks and jobs. She smiled, said "still waiting," and went to sit on the back steps. Her first thought was the old one: I'm not good enough. Her friend Jagdish, who had come with his family, found her there. "Tell me what actually happened this semester," he said. So she did, out loud. Seven courses instead of the usual five, because she'd wanted to finish early. Reading the textbook twice and never testing herself. "So," Jagdish said, "too heavy a load, and a way of studying that doesn't work for you." Irawati turned it over. It sounded different from not good enough. It sounded like information. By the time lunch was called, she had two lines in her phone: five courses next term. Practice questions, not rereading.

qa.q: How many courses did Irawati take this semester?
qa.a: Seven courses instead of the usual five.

qa.q: What was Irawati's first thought on seeing the results?
qa.a: Irawati felt a familiar sting of inadequacy, thinking she wasn't good enough.

qa.q: What else could Irawati do next term?
qa.a: Irawati could check with an advisor that five courses fits the backlog plan, and test herself weekly to be sure the new method works.

qa.q: How does Jagdish help Irawati see the failure?
qa.a: Jagdish asks what happened and names the facts plainly, helping her see the failure as information rather than proof she isn't good enough.

grounding: Shows a student reframing a failed term as information, a too-heavy course load and a study method that needs changing, so planning can happen without self-blame.

subtype: Approach: reframing failure as a redirect [Thinking]
passage: The café near Kunal's Hyderabad campus was nearly empty at four. Kunal pushed his marksheet across the table to Samir: three failed subjects. "I'm just not cut out for engineering." Samir didn't argue. He asked, "What was different this semester?" Kunal thought. "I took two extra electives to look good for placements. And I switched to watching lecture videos at double speed instead of doing problems." "So you tried to carry eight subjects and changed how you study." Kunal frowned at the sheet. Put like that, it didn't sound like a verdict on him. It sounded like a report on his choices. He took the pen from Samir's pocket and wrote on the back of the marksheet: "Load too heavy. Method wrong." Under it: "Next term: six subjects. Problems every day, videos only when stuck." His shoulders dropped a little. "That's a plan I can actually make," he said.

qa.q: What did Kunal write on the back of the marksheet?
How did Kunal feel at the start?
qa.a: Kunal felt defeated and full of self-blame, saying he was not cut out for engineering.

qa.q: What else could Kunal do to check the new method is working?
qa.a: Kunal could take a short self-test every two weeks, so he knows early whether daily problems are helping.
Samir asks what was different instead of arguing, which helps Kunal see the failure as information about choices, not ability.

grounding: Illustrates a student reframing a failed term as a sign that the load was too heavy and the method needs changing, which lets planning happen without self-blame.
